title: How Motivation Relates to Generative AI Use: A Large-Scale Survey of Mexican High School Students
extended_summary:
This paper investigates how high school students’ motivational profiles relate to their use of generative AI tools in learning, with a particular focus on math and writing. The authors argue that students are not a uniform group in how they approach AI and that differences in self-concept and perceived subject value may shape whether students use AI for support, refinement, or shortcut-seeking. The study is motivated by broader concerns and hopes around generative AI in education, including personalized help, immediate feedback, academic integrity, and cognitive offloading.

The study uses a large-scale anonymous online survey rather than an intervention. Students reported their motivation in math and writing and their frequency of using generative AI for different tasks in each domain. In writing, these tasks included brainstorming ideas, producing outlines, finding supporting evidence, improving language and grammar, getting writing feedback, and adapting writing to requirements. The authors then applied K-means clustering to identify motivational profiles and compared AI usage patterns across those profiles.

Participants were 6,793 public high school students in the final two years of high school in Chihuahua, Mexico, drawn from an initial sample of 7,739 students after excluding failed attention checks and students with no prior generative AI experience. The instruments were administered in Spanish. The context was public high schools, but the data collection itself was conducted through an online survey, and the paper does not describe any classroom-based implementation of AI or teacher-led instructional program.

The main conclusion is that students with different motivational profiles use generative AI in systematically different ways, and that these patterns vary by subject domain. In writing, aspirational students tended to use AI more for brainstorming and outlining, confident students more for language/grammar improvement and writing feedback, and disengaged students reported the lowest overall writing-related AI use. The authors conclude that one-size-fits-all approaches to AI integration are inadequate and that more targeted, motivationally informed approaches are needed. The paper does not measure direct literacy outcomes or causal effects of AI use on learning.
quality_tier_rationale: Large-scale K-12 survey with clear methods and substantial sample size, but it is correlational and based on self-report rather than causal identification or direct learning outcomes.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not estimate learning impact or intervention effects; it documents heterogeneous usage patterns and attitudes, so educational impact is unclear.

interventions.use_case: Survey of Mexican high school students' self-reported use of generative AI tools for writing tasks such as brainstorming, outline production, language/grammar improvement, writing feedback, and requirement adaptation, as well as math help functions.
Generative AI used specifically as a writing assistant for brainstorming, outlining, grammar/language improvement, and writing feedback in high school writing tasks.

finding.finding_summary: The study examined self-reported patterns of generative AI use in writing, not literacy achievement. Students in different motivational clusters reported different writing-related uses of AI—for example, Confident students most often used AI for language/grammar improvement (M=2.79) and writing feedback (M=2.67), while Aspirational students most often used it for brainstorming (M=2.83) and outlining (M=2.72)—but no externally measured reading or writing outcomes, rubric-scored products, or error-reduction results were reported.
finding.measure: Self-reported frequency of AI use for writing-related tasks on a 1-5 Likert scale

finding.finding_summary: K-means clustering identified three motivational profiles in writing and math: Aspirational, Confident, and Disengaged. These profiles were associated with different AI usage patterns; in writing, Confident students reported the highest use for language/grammar improvement (M=2.79) and writing feedback (M=2.67), Aspirational students reported the highest use for brainstorming (M=2.83) and outlines (M=2.72), and Disengaged students reported the lowest overall writing-task AI use, indicating that AI engagement varies systematically with motivational profile rather than uniformly improving motivation.
finding.measure: Self-concept and perceived subject value surveys; self-reported AI usage frequencies by task
